c.tagline: Swahili coast crossroads of coral forts, spice-scented lanes and Indian Ocean beaches.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis are unmetered—agree a fare before setting off, or use Uber/Bolt for fixed in-app pricing. Tuk-tuks and matatus are far cheaper for short hops.

emergency.note: 999 and 112 both reach police, ambulance and fire; public response can be slow, so private ambulance services (e.g. St John, AAR) are widely used.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Caution in the Old Town and Likoni at night; petty crime on beaches (resorts patrolled)

hood_desc: The coral-stone Swahili quarter around Fort Jesus (a UNESCO World Heritage site), with carved wooden doors, narrow lanes and spice shops; the atmospheric historic heart of the island, best for culture on foot.
The commercial core around Moi Avenue and the iconic Mombasa Tusks, with markets, banks, offices and budget-to-midrange hotels; a convenient central base close to the Likoni ferry and Old Town.
A leafy upmarket suburb just north of the island with beach hotels, malls, expat restaurants and calm residential streets; the best balance of comfort and access to town.
A north-coast resort strip of white sand, all-inclusive beach hotels and the Haller Park nature trails; suits relaxed sun-and-sea holidays.
About 30km south across the Likoni ferry, a world-class 15km stretch of white sand and turquoise water lined with resorts, dive centres and beach bars; Mombasa's premier beach escape.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.hours: Matatus and tuk-tuks run roughly 5am-10pm with limited late service; the Likoni Ferry runs 24/7; ride-hailing operates 24/7 and is recommended after dark.
transit.note: There is no metro or urban rail; matatus and tuk-tuks handle most local trips and the Likoni Ferry links the island to the south coast, but heavy traffic and crowding lead many visitors to rely on ride-hailing apps.
transit.pay: Matatus and tuk-tuks are paid in cash to the conductor/driver, with M-Pesa mobile money increasingly accepted; the Likoni Ferry is free for foot passengers; SGR train tickets are bought at Mombasa Terminus or via the online portal. Ride-hailing apps (Uber, Bolt, Little Cab) are paid in-app.

train: Madaraka Express (SGR) to Nairobi from Mombasa Terminus

tip.r: Not obligatory; 5-10% at tourist restaurants or rounding up the bill is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Fort Jesus
This UNESCO-listed Portuguese fortress, built in 1593 to guard the Old Port, layers Portuguese, Omani, and British history behind coral-stone ramparts.
Mombasa Old Town
A labyrinth of carved Swahili doorways, balconied merchant houses, and centuries-old mosques where Arab, Indian, and African cultures intertwine beside the sea.
Mombasa Tusks
Four giant aluminium tusks arching over Moi Avenue, erected for Princess Elizabeth's 1952 visit, remain the city's most recognizable photo landmark.
Haller Park
A limestone quarry miraculously transformed into a lush sanctuary of giraffes, hippos, and giant tortoises, famed for the odd-couple friendship of Owen and Mzee.
Nyali Beach
Powder-white sands and palm-fringed resorts stretch along Mombasa's north shore, offering swimming, camel rides, and dhows drifting on the turquoise Indian Ocean.
Mandhry Mosque
Dating to the 16th century, one of Mombasa's oldest mosques raises its distinctive minaret over Old Town, still serving worshippers after 400-plus years.
Marikiti Market (Mackinnon Market)
Mombasa's sensory-overload central market heaps mangoes, spices, and coconuts under a colonial-era hall, the best place to taste coastal Kenya's flavors.
Jumba la Mtwana
Atmospheric 14th-century Swahili ruins of mosques and merchant houses crumble among baobabs right on the beach, a short trip north of the city.
Diani Beach
South of the Likoni ferry, this world-ranked stretch of flour-soft sand and reef-protected lagoon is coastal Kenya's ultimate beach day trip.
Mamba Village Centre
East Africa's largest crocodile farm lets you meet thousands of Nile crocodiles, ride camels, and tour botanical gardens in the Nyali suburbs.

train.note: No international trains - the SGR line stops at Naivasha and has never been extended to the Ugandan border for passengers. The Madaraka Express standard-gauge service between Mombasa and Nairobi is excellent value, taking about 6 hours in economy or first class, and is far better than the old metre-gauge train. Book on the Kenya Railways e-ticketing site or by M-Pesa; it sells out, especially at holidays. Mombasa Terminus is well outside the city, so allow for a taxi.

intl.to: Dar es Salaam (Tanzania) - via the Lunga Lunga border, ~8-10 hr

intl.op: Simba Coach / Tahmeed — tickets at the Mombasa terminals

bus.note: The Tanzania coaches cross at Lunga Lunga south of Mombasa, taking eight to ten hours to Dar es Salaam with a slow border stop - carry your passport and check the East African visa position, as a single-entry East Africa Tourist Visa covers Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda but not Tanzania. Domestically Modern Coast, Mash and Tahmeed run to Nairobi in about 8 hours and up the coast to Malindi in 2.

intl.to: Likoni (Kenya) - across Kilindini harbour to the south coast, free for pedestrians

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international passenger ferry - Mombasa's port is one of East Africa's main container terminals. The Likoni ferry, however, is essential transport: it is the only link between Mombasa island and the south coast beaches at Diani, carries thousands of people at a time and is free for foot passengers. Vehicle queues at rush hour can be very long.

half.name: Shimba Hills National Reserve
half.blurb: A forested reserve about ninety minutes southwest, the only place in Kenya to see sable antelope, with the Sheldrick Falls trail.

full.name: Tsavo East National Park
full.blurb: One of the world's largest game reserves about three hours away, known for red-dust elephants and wide open savanna.

full.name: Wasini Island
full.blurb: A small coral island about two hours south reached by dhow, with a coral garden boardwalk and dolphin-watching trips.
